transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Um, I came in because I've been having this issue lately. Well, once I start eating alone at night, it feels like something just takes over. I completely lose control and I can't stop. Even while I'm sitting there, literally telling myself in my head to put the food away, I just keep going.

After these episodes where you lose control and eat a lot, do you do anything to try to undo it or prevent weight gain—like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, exercising excessively, or restricting food the next day?

Yeah, I do. Um... after I eat like that, I usually end up going to the bathroom and making myself throw up. It just feels like the only way to undo it, you know? Like I have to get it out before the calories actually settle in.

When you have these episodes where you lose control and eat a lot, do you feel like you're eating an unusually large amount of food in a short period of time—like much more than most people would eat in that same timeframe?

Yeah, definitely. Um, especially on nights after my late shifts. I'll get home and just... I've eaten things like an entire frozen pizza, then cereal straight from the box, whatever leftovers are in the fridge, and just any snacks I can find in the cabinet. And that's all within maybe an hour or two. So, yeah, it's way more than I would ever eat in front of anyone else.
How often would you say these episodes of losing control and eating a lot happen? Like, is it happening multiple times a week, a few times a week, or at a different frequency?

Well, um... for at least the last four months, I'd say it happens usually at least once a week. There's at least one night each week where I'm alone and just end up eating way more than I ever meant to, and then... yeah, I make myself throw up afterward.

inference_history.note: Patient describes loss of control while eating alone at night with inability to stop despite conscious effort to restrain. This presentation is consistent with binge eating disorder (F50.81), bulimia nervosa (F50.2), impulse control disorder (F63.2), and other disorders involving loss of control. Further assessment needed regarding frequency, duration, associated behaviors (purging), distress level, and impact on functioning.

Patient describes binge eating with purging via self-induced vomiting, which is classic for bulimia nervosa (F50.2) or binge eating/purging subtype of anorexia nervosa (F50.81). Need to assess weight/BMI and eating restriction patterns to differentiate.

Ruled out F50.2 (Bulimia Nervosa). Patient presents with binge eating episodes followed by purging (self-induced vomiting), which is diagnostic for Binge Eating/Purging Type of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.81) or Bulimia Nervosa (F50.2). However, the patient has not mentioned restrictive eating patterns, low body weight, or intense fear of weight gain that would be central to anorexia nervosa. The clinical presentation of recurrent binge-purge cycles without mention of restrictive eating or body image disturbance specific to anorexia suggests F50.81 (Other specified feeding or eating disorder - binge eating/purging disorder) is more appropriate than F50.2 at this stage, though further clarification on body weight, body image, and eating patterns is needed.
